transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-19
Start: 16:30 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Alex, Priya, Jordan (Redwood) — Michael, Sasha, Leila (Stonehaven)

Summary (auto-ish):
Short: Stonehaven evaluating Redwood Private for production LLM inference; primary requirements are VPC-private connectivity, no public egress from inference nodes, support for cross-account PrivateLink or TGW peering, strict IP allowlists, and KMS/HSM key control. They are exploring Dedicated vs Private but leaning Private with a customer-managed dataplane. Next steps include sharing security artifacts and a follow-up bench with network details.

Topics: network topology, CIDR overlap, PrivateLink vs TGW/transit, IP whitelisting, egress NAT, region availability, audit logs, KMS integration, pilot sizing.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today, i'm alex from Redwood, uh, i'll kick us off and then priya will jump into the tech bits — michelle sorry michael, want to do quick intros real quick?
[00:12] Michael Ortiz: yea sure, i'm michael, head of infra at stonehaven, we run a multi-account aws setup, a bunch of data pipelines, and we're looking to host inference for customer-facing features, latency around 100–200ms target per request, and strict data residency requirements for eu and us-west.
[00:28] Sasha Roman: sasha here, security lead. main blockers for us are: no outbound public internet from inference hosts, full audit logs, and customer-controlled KMS. also we need IP allocation that fits our corporate ip plan.
[00:40] Priya Nair: got it. to clarify, when you say "no outbound public internet" do you mean nodes cannot have any route to 0.0.0.0/0 or you only want to prevent direct model downloads/telemetry?
[00:52] Leila Park: ideally no 0.0.0.0/0 from the inference subnets. we allow a NAT egress via a central egress account but traffic must be inspected and proxied through our infra.
[01:05] Jordan Li: okay that maps cleanly to support for private endpoints or transit gateway peering — different tradeoffs. quick question: are you ok with cross-account aws privatelink endpoints (interface ENIs in your VPC) or do you prefer full TGW peering where we stand up a transit?
[01:20] Michael Ortiz: depends on ops overhead. privatelink looks simpler for connectivity but we've had limits with ENI quotas in the past. TGW gives us central routing and NACL control. we also need support across us-west-2 and eu-west-1.
[01:36] Sasha Roman: also, how does redwood handle ip whitelisting for callbacks? our product uses signed webhooks and we want to allowlist only specific cidrs.
[01:45] Alex Chen: we can provide static egress IP ranges per deployment in Private mode; for Hosted there's different ranges. for private deployments, you can either peer via TGW or provision interface endpoints into your VPC. both work with allowlists.
[01:58] Leila Park: okay, can you explain the difference in failure modes? if our TGW link goes down what happens to inference traffic vs private link?
[02:08] Priya Nair: yeah so high-level — privatelink means traffic goes to an interface endpoint in your VPC, it's basically cross-account service endpoints. if the interface fails, we can failover to a fallback model variant or a different region depending on policy, but you still need path availability. TGW gives you a routed path through your transit fabric; if a single TGW attachment goes down, you can leverage secondary attachments or cross-region peering if set up. both need ops attention.
[02:36] Michael Ortiz: what about cidr overlap? we have 10.16.0.0/12 across multiple accounts. past vendors asked us to renumber which is a dealbreaker.
[02:46] Priya Nair: we support three patterns: 1) privatelink/interface endpoints — minimal routing changes and avoid CIDR overlap issues, 2) TGW/transit attachments where we request a non-overlapping range from you for the inference subnet, or 3) customer-managed NAT/proxy where you route to our peered proxy. so privatelink is often the easiest for overlapping CIDRs.
[03:06] Sasha Roman: and encryption — we need KMS keys retained in our account, HSM-backed preferred. how does redwood integrate?
[03:15] Alex Chen: for Private we can integrate with customer-managed KMS for at-rest disk encryption and for TLS client certs we can do mutual TLS. HSM-backed keys is something we support via cloud HSM integrations — we'll include that detail in the security pack.
[03:30] Leila Park: is there any agent or sidecar inside our VPC? we prefer not to install extra agents in prod.
[03:37] Jordan Li: no agent required for PrivateLink or TGW — the inference runtime lives in our private cluster in your secured network or in a customer-dataplane option. there's a lightweight control-plane connector but it's outbound-only from a management subnet that you control, and you can restrict it to your egress proxy. (little overlap with terms here)
[03:58] Michael Ortiz: you mentioned "customer-dataplane option" — can you expand?
[04:02] Priya Nair: sure. dedicated vs private: Dedicated is our reserved GPU pool in Redwood-managed infra but logically reserved for you; Private is where inference nodes are deployed into your VPC or into a private managed plane that sits behind your network controls. with Private you get more network control, KMS in your account, and stricter auditability.
[04:23] Sasha Roman: and logging — do we get token-level traces and full audit logs shipped to our splunk?
[04:30] Alex Chen: yes, we can push syslogs/audit logs to your collector via secure forwarders or into a customer S3 bucket with lifecycle rules. we can also emit structured traces to your observability endpoint.
[04:44] Leila Park: region coverage — we need eu-west-1 and us-west-2 for primary+failover. do you have private endpoints in those regions?
[04:54] Priya Nair: we can deploy Private in both regions. for on-prem or sovereign regions we have a package but that takes longer. for eu-west-1 and us-west-2, yes, reachable. we'll enumerate region-specific IP ranges in the followup doc.
[05:06] Michael Ortiz: any quota concerns for ENIs? last vendor hit our ENI limits during spike tests.
[05:14] Jordan Li: interface endpoints create ENIs in customer subnets; we'll size the number we need and can provide an ENI count estimate in the pilot. alternatively TGW avoids ENI pressure but requires unique CIDR.
[05:27] Sasha Roman: okay cost delta — is privatelink more expensive vs tgw?
[05:31] Alex Chen: privatelink tends to be simpler but has per-GB data charges on aws plus ENI costs; TGW has attachment costs and data processing charges too. we'll model that in the pilot based on your traffic shape.
[05:45] Leila Park: do you support split-horizon DNS or private hosted zone integration? we use internal names for endpoints.
[05:52] Priya Nair: yes, we can publish internal DNS records for interface endpoints and optionally integrate with your Route53 private hosted zones. there can be some ttl propagation caveats — we will document.
[06:05] Michael Ortiz: curious about failover behavior: if eu-west becomes unhealthy, can we fail to us-west without dropping sessions? we have long-running chat sessions with context kept on our side.
[06:18] Priya Nair: session continuity depends on where you store KV cache; if you keep the session state client-side and route requests to alternate region, it works. our runtime supports model fallbacks but not transparent cross-region session syncing unless you implement cross-region cache replication. we can recommend strategies.
[06:36] Sasha Roman: one more — firewall restrictions: we run deep packet inspection on egress. can you do mutual TLS and client cert pinning?
[06:45] Jordan Li: we support mTLS for data plane connections and mutual auth for control plane as well; cert pinning can be arranged via our enterprise controls. we'll add the specifics to the security doc.
[06:59] Michael Ortiz: do you have any examples of customers who did cross-account privatelink with heavy traffic? what were the gotchas?
[07:07] Alex Chen: yep — common gotchas: ENI quotas, security group rules blocking ephemeral ports, DNS resolution delays for private endpoints, and forgetting to update NACLs. Also clients sometimes forget to route VPC flow logs for troubleshooting. we've captured a checklist we can share.
[07:29] Leila Park: for onboarding, what's the typical timeline to production for a Private deployment?
[07:34] Priya Nair: usually 6–8 weeks for full private production: 1-2 weeks of scoping and security review, 2-3 weeks of network & infra provisioning and pilot, and 1-2 weeks of validation and rollout. can be faster if you re-use existing TGW peering and have pre-approved CIDRs.
[07:52] Sasha Roman: ok, procurement — what does the contract for Private look like? is there a platform fee?
[07:58] Alex Chen: Private typically is a platform license + managed support fee; Dedicated has reserved capacity commitments. we'll share the contract summary and pricing ranges after this call.
[08:08] Michael Ortiz: got it. let's talk specifics — i'll drop our CIDR ranges in the doc but we also want a network diagram. what precisely do you need?
[08:18] Alex Chen: please share: VPC IDs, primary subnets (with AZs), route tables screenshots, NAT/egress account details, any existing TGW attachments, and team contacts for firewall changes. also note any compliance/regulatory constraints per region.
[08:33] Leila Park: we have an existing transit hub in us-west-2 but not in eu-west-1, so we might have to create a separate attach. will that slow things?
[08:42] Priya Nair: not if we scope it early; we can run a split pilot where eu-west uses privatelink and us-west uses TGW initially.
[08:52] Michael Ortiz: latency targets again — we want p95 < 250ms from our app to inference and back including routing. can you provide bench numbers?
[08:59] Jordan Li: we'll run a bench test in the pilot and provide expected p95 per model size and token length. priya will supply a throughput map.
[09:08] Sasha Roman: any SSO/SSO integrations for admin console? we use okta with SAML 2.0 and SCIM for provisioning.
[09:15] Alex Chen: yes we support SAML SSO via Okta and SCIM for user provisioning. RBAC maps to roles and token scopes; we'll show a sample mapping.
[09:26] Leila Park: what about audit retention — we need 7 years for certain logs. do you support long-term retention?
[09:33] Priya Nair: we support shipping logs to your S3 buckets and you can enforce retention policies there; for in-platform retention we have tiers — we'll share options.
[09:43] Michael Ortiz: let's talk about the pilot: we want to run a low-volume pilot that mirrors production traffic shape. what do you need from us for that?
[09:51] Jordan Li: a small dataset, sample request profiles, token length distribution, and expected concurrency. also credentials for private connectivity testing and a test VPC with permissive rules.
[09:59] Sasha Roman: we don't want data to leave region X; for compliance reasons some PE requests must stay in eu-west-1. can you guarantee region affinity?
[10:08] Alex Chen: with Private you can pin region and model versions; we can enforce region routing policies and deny cross-region fallbacks unless you allow them. we'll explain the routing policy config.
[10:20] Leila Park: ok, one more thing — would you be able to provide a small runbook for ops in case of degraded performance?
[10:26] Priya Nair: absolutely, we'll include an ops runbook with troubleshooting steps, metrics to watch, and a playbook for failovers.
[10:33] Michael Ortiz: are there any minimum commitments? we are trying to avoid long-term vendor lock in.
[10:39] Alex Chen: pilot has no long-term commit; Dedicated has reserved commits but Private can be structured as subscription or contract dependent. we'll propose flexible pilot-friendly terms.
[10:49] Sasha Roman: does Redwood support private peering for GCP and Azure too? we do some workloads on GCP.
[10:55] Jordan Li: yes, multi-cloud is supported but with different primitives — GCP uses VPC peering or Private Service Connect, Azure uses Private Link. we'll map each to equivalent patterns.
[11:07] Leila Park: good. i'd like to capture the exact deliverables from Redwood after this call — can you list them now?
[11:12] Alex Chen: sure: 1) security pack (SOC2, KMS/HSM notes, mTLS details), 2) network checklist and example diagrams, 3) pilot sizing + cost estimate, 4) ops runbook, 5) contract summary. we'll send all in a single package within 2 business days.
[11:31] Michael Ortiz: perfect. for the bench, we'll plan for a 2-week pilot with small traffic. can priya start the bench once we share the sample traces?
[11:39] Priya Nair: yes — once we have traces and CIDRs we can spin up the pilot and run an initial load test.
[11:45] Sasha Roman: regarding the mTLS certs — do we need to provide certs or can you generate for us?
[11:50] Jordan Li: we can work either way; enterprise customers usually provide certs to keep control. if you want we can generate and transfer, but we'll document the best practice.
[11:58] Leila Park: anything else we should know?
[12:00] Alex Chen: just that we'll avoid asking you to renumber your whole network — privatelink helps with that. we'll put a recommended path for minimal infra changes.
[12:09] Michael Ortiz: thanks all, seems like good next step.
[12:12] Alex Chen: great — recap: alex to send security + network pack, leila to share VPC details, priya to prep pilot plan and bench. we'll schedule an hour follow-up for the week of 2027-05-24. any final questions?
[12:26] Sasha Roman: none here. thanks.
[12:29] Leila Park: thanks everyone.
[12:31] Jordan Li: thanks. bye.

(Transcript notes: occasional mislabels from automated transcription, e.g., "michelle" for michael early, and a few acronyms split — TGW sometimes expanded as "tee gee double you" in transcript.)
